name: Hazardous materials response
description: Placards, shipping papers, entry briefings, air monitoring, decontamination corridors, protective action orders and the structured decisions of a hazmat response. The pack does not include the text or the distance tables of the Emergency Response Guidebook: distances are typed by the facilitator from their own copy, or invented for a fictional material and labeled as exercise values. Stays at the coordination and decision level; not hazmat guidance for a real incident.
outsideParties: the 24-hour chemical emergency information line (fictional in the exercise)
the chemical facility and its emergency coordinator
the state environmental agency and the National Response Center

advisorRoles.name: Decontamination Unit Leader
advisorRoles.description: Sets up the corridor, controls who goes through it and hands decontaminated patients to the Medical Group.

advisorRoles.name: Entry Team Leader
advisorRoles.description: Leads the entry team at the technician level, reports readings and keeps to the abort criteria.

advisorRoles.name: Facility Emergency Coordinator
advisorRoles.description: Speaks for the chemical facility: what the material is, how much, and what the facility's own plan says.

decisionForms.label: Set isolation and protective actions
decisionForms.description: Choose the isolation zone and the downwind protective action, with the source of the distances.

fields.label: Source of the distances
choices: Entered from the facilitator's own guidebook edition
Invented exercise values for a fictional material

decisionForms.label: Set PPE level and authorize entry
decisionForms.description: The hazmat group chooses the protective level and sends an entry team with an objective and abort criteria.

glossary.definition: OSHA's emergency response levels: awareness, operations, technician, specialist and incident commander. Players act at their level; an operations-level crew does not enter the hot zone to stop a leak.
Hot zone (the release area), warm zone (decontamination), cold zone (command and support).
The initial isolation zone is a circle around the release. The protective action zone is a square downwind whose side is the protective action distance.
Two protective actions for people downwind; the choice depends on the material, the time available, the route and the people.
Four-digit identification number on the placard or orange panel and on the shipping paper.
Names the material (UN number, proper shipping name, class, packing group), the quantity and a 24-hour emergency phone; kept in the cab or with the crew.

productConventions: A placard shows the class number, a hazard word and the UN number; products print the word, never color alone.
A protective action order or recommendation always states the source of its distances.
The air monitoring log has time, place, instrument, reading, action level and result. Readings are invented exercise values.
realismRules: Never ship or invent Emergency Response Guidebook text or distance tables. Distances come from the facilitator's own guidebook, or belong to a fictional material and are labeled as invented exercise values.
Never pair a real UN number with distances the author made up; use a fictional material for invented distances.
Players use their own guidebook for decisions; the exercise is not a source of real hazmat guidance.
Responders act at their trained level and wait for the technician team when they are only operations level.
The wind is stated with its source and time, and a wind shift forces the protective action to be revisited.
Decontamination comes before patients reach the ambulances; the hospital is told what the material is.
Identification comes from the placard, the shipping paper and the facility, and may disagree at first.
Stay at who decides what; no entry techniques or neutralization steps.
